items.prompt: What does the idiom a piece of cake mean?

options.text: a small snack
options.why: This is the literal meaning, not the idiom.

options.text: something very easy
a birthday present
options.why: The idiom is not about presents.

options.text: something very sweet
options.why: The idiom is not about taste.

hints: An idiom does not mean exactly what its words say.
Think about how easy it is to eat a piece of cake.
Try it in a sentence: The test was a piece of cake.
items.explanation: If something is a piece of cake, it is very easy, as easy as eating cake.

items.prompt: Match each idiom to its meaning.
hints: Idioms are fixed phrases with a hidden meaning.
Picture each phrase, then think about the feeling or action it suggests.
Start with over the moon. Would you feel happy or sad up there?
items.explanation: Over the moon means very happy, under the weather means ill and break the ice means start talking. Hit the books means study, on the same page means agreeing and let off steam means release energy.

items.prompt: In which sentence is cold feet used as an idiom?

options.text: Lani’s feet were cold after swimming.
options.why: Here the words have their literal meaning.

options.text: Wear socks or you will get cold feet.
options.why: This is literal: your feet would really be cold.

options.text: Lani got cold feet before the speech contest and nearly stayed at home.
The cold floor made our feet freeze.
options.why: This describes real cold feet.

hints: The idiom to get cold feet is about a feeling, not temperature.
Look for a sentence where someone becomes nervous about doing something.
Ask of each sentence: are the feet really cold?
items.explanation: To get cold feet means to become nervous and want to back out. Lani nearly stayed at home because she was nervous.

items.prompt: The classroom was a beehive of activity. What does this metaphor suggest?

options.text: Everyone was busy.
There were real bees in the classroom.
options.why: This is a metaphor, so it is not literal.

options.text: The classroom was sweet and sticky.
options.why: The comparison is about how busy bees are, not honey.

options.text: The pupils were angry.
options.why: Bees can sting, but this comparison is about busy movement.

hints: Think about what a beehive is like inside.
The metaphor compares the classroom to a beehive.
Ask: what are bees in a hive always doing?
items.explanation: A beehive is full of bees busily working. The metaphor suggests that everyone in the classroom was busy.

items.prompt: Complete the idiom. Don’t count your chickens before they ___.
hints: The idiom is about eggs that have not opened yet.
It warns you not to be sure of something before it happens.
What do chicks do when they come out of their eggs?
items.explanation: Don’t count your chickens before they hatch means do not be sure of a good result until it has actually happened.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences into literal and figurative.

items.text: My heart sank when I saw the score.
The stone sank to the bottom.
The knife has a sharp edge.
He is the apple of his gran’s eye.
We picked apples from the tree.

hints: Literal means the words mean exactly what they say.
Ask: could this really happen in the way it is written?
Start with the stone. Can a stone really sink?
items.explanation: A stone can really sink and a knife can really be sharp, so those are literal. A heart cannot really sink, so that sentence is figurative: it means feeling disappointed.

items.prompt: The old house groaned and shivered in the storm. Why has the writer used personification?

options.text: to tell us the exact age of the house
options.why: The sentence does not give its age.

options.text: to make the house seem alive and show how strong the storm was
to show that the people inside were ill
options.why: The house is described, not the people.

options.text: to explain how houses are built
options.why: This is description, not explanation.

hints: Groaned and shivered are things people do.
Think about why a person might groan and shiver.
Ask: what does this tell you about the storm outside?
items.explanation: Giving the house human actions makes it seem alive and suffering, which shows how powerful the storm was.

items.prompt: Read: The city was a giant machine. Its roads were conveyor belts, and its people were tiny gears that never stopped turning. What does this extended metaphor suggest?

options.text: The city is busy, organised and never stops.
The city is quiet and relaxing.
options.why: Machines and turning gears suggest constant movement.

options.text: The city is broken and needs fixing.
options.why: The machine in the metaphor is working, not broken.

options.text: The city has many factories.
options.why: The whole city is compared to a machine. It does not say there are factories.

hints: An extended metaphor continues the same comparison over several sentences.
Think about what a machine with belts and gears is like.
Ask: is a working machine busy or still?
items.explanation: The writer compares the whole city to a machine. Conveyor belts and gears that never stop suggest a busy, organised place that keeps going all the time.

items.prompt: Choose all the idioms that mean someone is very nervous.

options.text: had butterflies in my stomach
was over the moon
options.why: This means very happy.

options.text: had my heart in my mouth
was as cool as a cucumber
options.why: This means calm.

options.text: was shaking like a leaf

hints: Think about how your body feels when you are nervous.
Some idioms describe a fluttery stomach, a racing heart or trembling.
Cross out the idioms for happy and calm feelings first.
items.explanation: Butterflies in your stomach, your heart in your mouth and shaking like a leaf all describe feeling very nervous or frightened.

items.prompt: Choose the idiom that best completes the sentence. Rafi kept the surprise party a secret for weeks, but his little sister ___ at breakfast.

options.text: hit the nail on the head
options.why: This means said something exactly right.

options.text: kept her head above water
options.why: This means managed to cope with difficulties.

options.text: bit off more than she could chew
options.why: This means tried to do too much.

options.text: let the cat out of the bag

hints: The sentence tells you that a secret was kept for weeks.
Something happened to the secret at breakfast.
Look for the idiom that means telling a secret by mistake.
items.explanation: To let the cat out of the bag means to tell a secret by mistake, which is what the little sister did.

items.prompt: Kofi says, It is raining cats and dogs. What does he mean?

options.text: Cats and dogs are falling from the sky.
options.why: This is the literal picture. Idioms do not mean exactly what the words say.

options.text: It is raining only a little.
options.why: The idiom is about heavy rain, not light rain.

options.text: It is raining very hard.
Pets are playing in the rain.
options.why: The idiom is not about pets.

hints: An idiom has a hidden meaning.
Think about how strong the rain must be for such a funny phrase.
Cats and dogs cannot really fall. So the phrase is about the rain itself.
items.explanation: Raining cats and dogs is an idiom for very heavy rain. Animals do not really fall.

items.prompt: When Wulan won the prize, she was over the ___. Her friends were ___ happy for her.
hints: Over the ___ is a very common idiom about joy.
The idiom names something far above the Earth.
The second gap needs a word that fits the happy mood.
items.explanation: Over the moon means extremely happy. Really happy fits the same cheerful mood.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences into literal and figurative.

items.text: Tom spilled the beans about the party.
Tom spilled beans on the kitchen floor.
The quiz was a tough nut to crack.
Amara cracked a nut with a stone.
Citra has a heart of gold.
The ring is made of gold.

hints: Literal means the words are true as they are written.
Figurative means the words stand for another idea.
Ask whether the sentence could be photographed exactly as it is written.
items.explanation: Beans on a floor, a cracked nut and a gold ring are real things. Revealing a secret, a hard problem and a kind person are figurative ideas.

items.prompt: Match each metaphor to what it suggests about the subject.
pairs: Time takes things from us without us noticing.
The room was noisy and wild.
Her voice was soft and smooth.
Life has a path with different stages.
He is a rock for his family.
hints: A metaphor says one thing IS another to show a quality.
Think about what the second thing is famous for.
Start with the zoo. What happens in a zoo?
items.explanation: Each metaphor borrows a quality from the second thing: a thief takes, a zoo is wild, velvet is smooth, a journey has stages and a rock is strong.

items.prompt: In which sentence is the idiom break a leg used literally?

options.text: Good luck in the school play. Break a leg!
options.why: Here it is an idiom that wishes someone good luck.

options.text: Leo fell off his skateboard and might break a leg.
Before her solo, Yuki’s friends told her to break a leg.
options.why: This is the good-luck idiom.

options.text: The coach told us to break a leg on the field today.
options.why: Here it is also used as the idiom for good luck.

hints: Literal means the words are true as they are written.
Look for a sentence about a real injury.
Check which sentence is about a skateboard accident, not about luck.
items.explanation: Only the skateboard sentence is about a real leg that could really break. In the others, break a leg wishes someone good luck.

items.prompt: Complete the idiom. Maya accidentally let the cat out of the ___.
hints: This idiom is about telling a secret by mistake.
The cat was hidden inside something that you can carry.
It is something you might put shopping in.
items.explanation: To let the cat out of the bag means to reveal a secret by accident.

items.prompt: Build a metaphor, not a simile, to describe a kind smile. Use the cards.
hints: A metaphor does not use like or as.
The sentence says one thing was another thing.
Start with the person, then the thing being described.
items.explanation: A metaphor says one thing is another, so there is no like or as. Her smile was pure sunshine shows warmth and brightness.

items.prompt: Sort each sentence by the figure of speech it uses.
hints: Personification gives human actions to things.
A simile uses like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another.
Look at the first sentence. Can wind whisper like a person?
items.explanation: Whispering is a human action, so that is personification. A bell is stated as the laugh, so it is a metaphor. As fast as uses as, so it is a simile.

items.text: The wind whispered through the trees.
Her laugh was a bright bell.
The runner was as fast as a cheetah.

items.prompt: Read: Life is a river. Bayu was now at the rapids, and his friends were the rocks he held on to. What do the rapids suggest?

options.text: a fast and difficult part of life
a calm and peaceful time
options.why: Rapids are rough water, not calm water.

options.text: a holiday by the water
options.why: The river is a picture for life, not a real trip.

options.text: the end of a story
options.why: Rapids are in the middle of a river, so this is not about an ending.

hints: The whole passage is one comparison: life is a river.
Think about what rapids are like for a boat.
Rough, fast water stands for something in Bayu’s life.
items.explanation: Rapids are fast, rough water. In the extended metaphor they stand for a hard, stressful time, and friends are the support he holds on to.

items.prompt: Read: The debate was a battlefield. Rangga fired his best argument, but Sekar blocked it with a strong shield of facts. Which words continue the battlefield metaphor?

options.text: Rangga and Sekar
options.why: These are only the names of the speakers.

options.text: best and strong
options.why: These are adjectives and do not belong to a battle.

options.text: debate and facts
options.why: Debate and facts are the real subjects, not battle images.

options.text: fired and shield

hints: An extended metaphor keeps using words from one picture.
The picture here is a battle.
Which words would you hear in a real fight?
items.explanation: Fired and shield come from the world of battle, so they extend the metaphor across the sentences.

items.prompt: Choose all the sentences that use the idiom in a figurative way.

options.text: We went for a walk in the park after lunch.
options.why: This is a real walk in a real park.

options.text: Hadi was on thin ice after he arrived late again.
Tom hit the sack early because he was tired.
The ice on the lake was too thin to walk on.
options.why: Here thin ice is real, so the meaning is literal.

options.text: Dewi’s mum said the test was a walk in the park.

hints: Figurative means the phrase stands for another idea.
Decide if a real park, real ice or a real sack is being described.
Try to replace each idiom with a plain meaning such as easy, in danger, or went to bed.
items.explanation: A walk in the park means easy, thin ice means in a risky position, and hit the sack means went to bed. The other two sentences describe real things.

items.prompt: Tara tiptoed around her grumpy brother all morning. Which idiom best describes how she acted?

options.text: walking on air
options.why: This means feeling extremely happy.

options.text: walking on eggshells
walking the plank
options.why: This idiom is about facing a dangerous punishment.

options.text: walking in circles
options.why: This means getting nowhere.

hints: Tiptoeing means moving very carefully.
Which idiom is about being careful not to upset someone?
Think about what happens if you step on an eggshell.
items.explanation: Walking on eggshells means being very careful so you do not make someone angry. It matches Tara tiptoeing around her brother.

items.prompt: Worry was a tide. Some mornings it drained away, and other nights it flooded the whole beach of his mind. What does the extended metaphor show?

options.text: that he enjoys swimming at the beach
options.why: The beach is not real here. It is a picture of his mind.

options.text: that his worry stays the same size all day
options.why: A tide rises and falls, so the worry changes.

options.text: that his worry comes and goes and can feel overwhelming
that the sea is dangerous at night
options.why: The writer is describing feelings, not the sea.

hints: Look at what a tide really does.
Match each part: tide, drained, flooded, beach.
The beach stands for his mind, so the flood stands for something that fills it.
items.explanation: A tide rises and falls. The metaphor shows worry that goes away and returns, sometimes filling his whole mind.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the idiom incorrectly?

options.text: The two friends buried the hatchet and shook hands.
options.why: Bury the hatchet means make peace, so this use is correct.

options.text: After the long quarrel, Ines and Leo decided to bury the hatchet.
options.why: This is a correct use meaning make peace.

options.text: Let us bury the hatchet and be friends again.
options.why: This is also a correct use of the idiom.

options.text: The two friends buried the hatchet and started arguing again.

hints: Bury the hatchet is about ending a fight.
Look for a sentence where the idiom and the result do not agree.
Check which sentence says peace was made but then something opposite happens.
items.explanation: To bury the hatchet means to stop fighting and make peace. Starting an argument right after is the opposite meaning.

items.prompt: An old story says: "I bid you good morrow." What does good morrow mean?

options.text: good night
options.why: Morrow is not about night.

options.text: goodbye
options.why: It is a greeting, not a farewell.

options.text: good morning
good luck
options.why: Morrow does not mean luck.

hints: The phrase is old and no longer common.
Use the situation: it is a greeting.
Think of the word tomorrow.
items.explanation: Morrow is an old word for morning or the next day. Good morrow is an old way to say good morning.

items.prompt: Read: "By and by, the rain stopped and the sun came out." What does by and by mean?

options.text: next to each other
options.why: By and by is not about position.

options.text: after a while
straight away
options.why: By and by describes time passing, not instant.

options.text: never
options.why: The rain stopped, so something happened.

hints: Look at the order of events.
The rain stopped some time later.
By and by shows time passing.
items.explanation: By and by is an older phrase meaning after a short time.

items.prompt: Read: "The cat paced to and fro across the room." What does to and fro mean?

options.text: up and down the stairs
options.why: Stairs are not mentioned.

options.text: out of the room
options.why: The cat stays across the room.

options.text: back and forth
round in a circle
options.why: To and fro is a straight movement in two directions.

hints: A cat is pacing.
Pacing means going the same way again and again.
Picture the cat walking one way and then the other.
items.explanation: To and fro means back and forth.

items.prompt: Read: "The crowd waited with bated breath for the result." What does bated breath suggest?

options.text: They were holding their breath with worry or excitement
They were breathing very loudly
options.why: Bated breath is quiet, not loud.

options.text: They were out of breath after running
options.why: The crowd is waiting, not running.

options.text: They were bored
options.why: Bated breath shows strong feeling.

hints: Bated is an old word meaning held back.
What do people do when they are very nervous?
Look at the word waited.
items.explanation: Bated breath describes holding back your breath because you are tense or excited.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a metaphor to make the fog feel mysterious?

options.text: The fog was as thick as soup.
options.why: This is a simile because it uses as.

options.text: The fog was thick.
options.why: This is a plain description.

options.text: The fog was a grey ghost creeping over the fields.
The fog came at six o'clock.
options.why: This gives a time, not a picture.

hints: A metaphor says something is something else.
Look for the sentence with no like or as.
Which one gives the fog the feeling of a ghost?
items.explanation: The fog was a grey ghost is a metaphor. It helps the reader feel the mystery.

items.prompt: Complete the simile to show how loud the noise was. The crash was ___ a clap of thunder.
hints: A simile compares two things using like or as.
The noise was loud.
Choose the phrase that compares loudness.
items.explanation: As loud as a clap of thunder compares the crash with thunder.
